transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... honestly, I just can't shake this feeling lately. It's like this heavy weight, you know? I just... I can't stop feeling like everything that goes wrong is entirely my fault. It's exhausting. Like, at work, I'm a business operations specialist, and if a project gets delayed or even if there's just a minor hiccup in the supply chain, I immediately think, 'This is because of me. I messed up. I'm a terrible employee.' And it doesn't stop there. It bleeds into everything. I just bought this house not too long ago, which was supposed to be this big, exciting milestone, right? But instead, if a pipe leaks or the lawn looks bad, I just spiral. I start thinking I'm a horrible homeowner, that I'm irresponsible, and that I honestly deserve to lose everything I've worked so hard for. It's just this constant, overwhelming guilt that I'm ruining everything I touch, and I don't know how to turn it off.
How long have you been feeling this way—has it been a matter of weeks, or has this guilt and low mood been going on for two years or more?

Well, it's definitely not just a matter of weeks, I can tell you that much. Um, it's been going on for a really long time. I actually remember exactly when it started, because it was right around the time I was trying to transition into a new role at my old company, and everything just felt so overwhelming, and that was... gosh, about two years and one month ago. Yes, two years and one month. I remember it was just after my birthday, and I thought, 'Oh, this is just a phase, you know, just stress from the job,' but the depression and this complete loss of interest in, well, everything, it just never went away. It settled in like this permanent fog. I used to love doing things, like I used to go hiking every weekend, and I loved cooking, but for the last two years and a month, I just... I haven't cared about any of it. I'd come home from work and just stare at the wall, feeling this crushing weight, and thinking about how I'm just failing at life. So, yeah, it's been a very long, very exhausting two years and one month of just feeling completely empty and guilty all the time.

Over these past two years, has your low mood and guilt been present nonstop every day, or have there been stretches of weeks or months where you felt back to your normal self before the symptoms returned?

Well, it definitely hasn't been like, you know, a few days here and there where I feel bad and then I bounce back. It's... it's been pretty much constant. I mean, looking back at it all, the low mood and just not caring about anything, it's been there for almost the entire time since this all started. Like, it's just this heavy blanket over everything. There might have been, I don't know, a few very brief periods where I could function a little better? Like, maybe a few days where I managed to actually get out of bed without it feeling like a monumental task, or I was able to get through a whole workday without completely spiraling about some tiny mistake on a spreadsheet. But even then, it wasn't like I was back to my normal self. Not at all. It was more like... like treading water instead of actively drowning, if that makes sense. The guilt is always kind of humming in the background, just waiting to get loud again. So, yeah, no long stretches of feeling normal. Just maybe a few days here and there where the fog wasn't quite as thick, but it's always there. Always. It's just exhausting to even think about how long it's been like this, honestly.
During this two-year period, have you ever experienced thoughts that life isn't worth living or thoughts of harming yourself?

No, no, I haven't... I haven't had thoughts like that. I know it sounds like I might, with how heavy everything feels, but honestly, it's more just this constant, exhausting guilt. Like, I'll be lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, thinking about how I forgot to email a vendor back, and I just feel this crushing sense of failure, but it never crosses over into wanting to... you know, end things or hurt myself. It's more of a feeling that I'm just doing everything wrong and that I don't deserve the good things I have, like my house or my job. I mean, my job is stressful enough, being a business operations specialist, there's always something going wrong, always a fire to put out, and I just take it all so personally. But even on the worst days, when I'm just crying in my car after work because a shipment got delayed and I'm convinced my boss thinks I'm incompetent, I don't think about harming myself. I just think about how I can try to fix it, even though I feel like I can't fix anything. So, yeah, no thoughts of not wanting to be here, just... just a lot of thoughts about how bad I am at being here, if that makes sense. I just want to feel better, I want to be able to enjoy my life again without this constant weight.
During this two-year period, have you also noticed significant changes in your sleep or appetite, or trouble concentrating, along with the low mood and guilt?

Well, my sleep has been... honestly, it's been an absolute nightmare. I mean, my appetite hasn't really changed much, and my concentration at work is, you know, okay enough to get by, even though I'm always second-guessing myself. But the sleep... gosh, the sleep is just awful. Most nights, I just lie there. I'll get into bed at a reasonable hour, maybe ten o'clock, thinking, 'Okay, tonight's the night I'm going to get a full eight hours,' but then I just lie awake. I'll lie there for hours, just listening to the house settle. You know how older houses have those little creaks and groans? I hear every single one of them. I'll hear the refrigerator hum kick on, I'll hear a car drive by three streets over, and my brain just will not shut off. I'll be thinking about that vendor email I mentioned, or worrying if I filed that one invoice in the right folder. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off, which usually isn't until maybe one or two in the morning, I almost always wake up again around three or four. And once I'm up at three or four, that's it. I'm awake. I can't get back to sleep no matter what I try. I've tried reading, I've tried drinking warm milk, I've tried those little meditation apps on my phone where the guy has a really soothing voice, but nothing works. I just lie there in the dark, watching the clock tick closer and closer to when my alarm is supposed to go off for work. And then by the time I actually have to get up and get ready for the office, I'm just completely exhausted. It makes the whole day feel so much harder to get through, dragging myself to my desk and trying to look at spreadsheets when I've only had maybe two or three hours of broken sleep. It's just... it's been like this for so long, and it really just amplifies all that guilt and heaviness I was telling you about. It's like a vicious cycle, you know? I can't sleep because I'm worried and feeling guilty, and then I feel worse the next day because I haven't slept.
Have you or others noticed that you're moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or conversely feeling physically restless and unable to sit still, during this period?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because I don't feel restless at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite. It's like... like everything is just dragged down. I don't know if other people have noticed, honestly, because I try so hard to hide it at work, but I feel it constantly. Especially in the mornings. I'll get to my desk, and just the physical act of getting started is exhausting. I'll sit there, and opening a spreadsheet—something I do fifty times a day—feels like it takes monumental effort. My hands just feel heavy. Typing responses to emails... it's like my fingers don't want to cooperate, like I'm typing in slow motion. 

And walking... gosh, walking to a meeting down the hall feels like I'm pushing through wet cement. I can feel how slow I'm moving, and I'll be thinking in my head, 'Hurry up, walk faster, people are going to notice,' but my body just won't listen. It's like there's this disconnect between my brain telling me to move and my limbs actually doing it. I used to be the kind of person who would just zip around the office, you know? Grabbing printouts, popping over to someone's cubicle to ask a quick question instead of messaging them. But now, I just dread having to get up. I'll put off going to the bathroom or getting a glass of water just because the thought of physically standing up and walking those twenty feet feels so incredibly draining. It's just this heavy, sluggish feeling that settles into my bones, and it takes so much energy just to do the bare minimum physical movements required to get through the day. So, yeah, definitely not restless. Just... incredibly, incredibly slow.

Has this depression affected your ability to function at work or in your relationships to the point where you've missed work, avoided social situations, or had any unusual experiences like hearing things others don't or having beliefs that others find strange?

Well, yeah... it's definitely affected things. I mean, I haven't had any of those unusual experiences you mentioned, like hearing things or having strange beliefs. It's really just the depression and how heavy everything is. But as far as functioning goes... gosh, it's just been so hard. I try so hard to keep it together, but I've definitely been avoiding social situations. Like, my friends will invite me out for dinner or drinks after work, and I just can't do it. I'll make up excuses, say I'm too tired or I have a headache, because the thought of sitting there and trying to pretend I'm okay, trying to keep up with the conversation and smile when I just feel so incredibly empty and guilty inside... it's just too much. So I just stay home. 

And even at home, things are slipping. I have this townhouse, and I usually take a lot of pride in keeping it nice, but lately, it's just gotten so messy. There are dishes piling up in the sink, laundry sitting in the basket for weeks, and I just look at it and feel even worse about myself, but I can't find the energy to clean it. It's like the mess is just another reminder of how much I'm failing. 

And work... work is where I really feel it. I haven't actually called out or missed days, because I'm so terrified of losing my job, but my performance is definitely suffering. I've been making mistakes, stupid little mistakes that I never used to make. Like, I'll enter the wrong shipping code on an order, or I'll forget to CC a department head on an important update. It got to the point where my supervisor actually pulled me aside and started checking in on me, asking if everything was okay because my error rate was up. That was humiliating. It just reinforced all that guilt I feel. I'm still there, I'm still doing the job, but it takes every ounce of effort I have just to keep up with the basic responsibilities. Everything just feels like it takes ten times more energy than it used to, and I'm just constantly terrified that I'm going to drop a major ball and get fired. It's exhausting.

Before this current two-year period began, had you ever experienced a distinct episode of depression in the past—one that later fully resolved and let you return to feeling like your normal self for a while?

No, not really... I mean, I've been trying to think back to before all this started, and I can't really think of anything like that. Before these last two years, I was actually doing pretty well. I mean, sure, I had normal stress, like anyone else. When I was finishing up my bachelor's degree, there were definitely times I felt completely overwhelmed with finals and trying to figure out what I was going to do with my life. And then starting my job as a business operations specialist... gosh, that was a huge learning curve. I remember my first few months at the company, I was so anxious about making a good impression and learning all the internal systems that I'd stay late almost every single night. 

But even then, even when I was stressed or tired from working long hours, it was never like *this*. It was just normal life stuff, you know? I never had a period where I felt this heavy, awful guilt and sluggishness that just took over my entire life, and then went away. Like, I've never had a time where I sank into a hole like this and then climbed back out and felt totally normal again. It really just feels like... like right around two years ago, this massive, heavy cloud just rolled in, and it's just stayed parked right over my head ever since. 

I really can't point to any time before that where I felt this way and then got better. I was just... normal. I'd go to work, I'd come home, I'd actually enjoy keeping my townhouse tidy, I'd go out with my friends on the weekends without dreading it or making up excuses. I actually had energy. So, no, I haven't had anything like this in the past that just came and went. This is really the first time my life has ever felt this incredibly heavy, and it just... it just hasn't stopped.

Thinking back... yeah, I mean, I really have racked my brain about this, probably more than I should. Because you'd think, right? You'd think there would be some warning sign or some earlier time in my life where I felt even a fraction of this, just to kind of prepare me or give me a clue that my brain could do this. But... no. Honestly, no. 

I look back at my teenage years, and I was just a completely standard teenager. I went to dances, I complained about my parents' rules, I worked a part-time job at a little boutique... I never had periods where I couldn't get out of bed or felt this overwhelming, crushing guilt. I was just normal. And then in college... like I was saying before about getting my bachelor's, there was definitely stress. I remember my junior year, I had to take this incredibly intense data analytics seminar, and I was so overwhelmed I literally called my mom hyperventilating, crying my eyes out, saying I was going to fail and drop out and ruin my life. But that lasted, what, maybe a day? I got a good night's sleep, I drank a giant iced coffee the next morning, and I went to the library and just figured it out. It completely resolved. It wasn't depression, it was just... being twenty and stressed about a syllabus. 

And then I went right back to being my normal, hyper-organized self. I was always the friend who planned all our weekend trips, you know? I'd make the detailed itineraries, I'd research the restaurants, I'd book the Airbnbs and figure out the split costs... I had so much energy for all of that. I actually loved doing it. It gave me joy. So there was never a time, not even a brief one, where I just shut down and stopped functioning, or felt this awful, sluggish heaviness, and then magically got better. There was no mini-episode or practice run for this. It's really just this one, long, horrible stretch that started two years ago and never lifted. Before that... I was honestly just fine. I was completely, boringly fine.

And then by the time I actually have to get up and get ready for the office, I'm just completely exhausted. It makes the whole day feel so much harder to get through, dragging myself to my desk and trying to look at spreadsheets when I've only had maybe two or three hours of broken sleep. It's just... it's been like this for so long, and it really just amplifies all that guilt and heaviness I was telling you about. It's like a vicious cycle, you know? I can't sleep because I'm worried and feeling guilty, and then I feel worse the next day because I haven't slept.

inference.note: Chronic (>2 years) nearly continuous depressive symptoms with insomnia and guilt, no discrete remission periods and no episodic mood elevation reported, consistent with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) rather than recurrent MDD (F33.9), which typically involves distinct episodes with intervening remission.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychomotor changes (agitation or retardation) to further establish criteria for persistent depressive symptoms consistent with dysthymia/PDD
doctor.question: Have you or others noticed that you're moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or conversely feeling physically restless and unable to sit still, during this period?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: At work I move so slowly some mornings that opening spreadsheets, typing responses, or walking to a meeting feels like I’m pushing through wet cement.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about moving or speaking more slowly than usual or feeling physically restless, which directly corresponds to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Well, it's funny you ask that, because I don't feel restless at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite. It's like... like everything is just dragged down. I don't know if other people have noticed, honestly, because I try so hard to hide it at work, but I feel it constantly. Especially in the mornings. I'll get to my desk, and just the physical act of getting started is exhausting. I'll sit there, and opening a spreadsheet—something I do fifty times a day—feels like it takes monumental effort. My hands just feel heavy. Typing responses to emails... it's like my fingers don't want to cooperate, like I'm typing in slow motion. 

And walking... gosh, walking to a meeting down the hall feels like I'm pushing through wet cement. I can feel how slow I'm moving, and I'll be thinking in my head, 'Hurry up, walk faster, people are going to notice,' but my body just won't listen. It's like there's this disconnect between my brain telling me to move and my limbs actually doing it. I used to be the kind of person who would just zip around the office, you know? Grabbing printouts, popping over to someone's cubicle to ask a quick question instead of messaging them. But now, I just dread having to get up. I'll put off going to the bathroom or getting a glass of water just because the thought of physically standing up and walking those twenty feet feels so incredibly draining. It's just this heavy, sluggish feeling that settles into my bones, and it takes so much energy just to do the bare minimum physical movements required to get through the day. So, yeah, definitely not restless. Just... incredibly, incredibly slow.

inference.note: Added F33.1/F33.2 given the presence of full depressive episode criteria (persistent guilt, psychomotor retardation, severe insomnia) sustained nearly continuously for over two years, suggesting a chronic/persistent major depressive episode rather than pure dysthymia; F34.1 retained given the two-year duration without clear symptom-free intervals.

doctor.intent: Assess the overall severity and functional impairment of the depressive episode (e.g., whether it's significantly impairing work/social functioning or involves any psychotic features) to differentiate moderate vs. severe major depressive episode
doctor.question: Has this depression affected your ability to function at work or in your relationships to the point where you've missed work, avoided social situations, or had any unusual experiences like hearing things others don't or having beliefs that others find strange?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve missed social plans, let the townhouse get messier than I can stand, and made enough mistakes at work that my supervisor started checking in on my performance. I’m still working, but it takes much more effort to keep up with basic responsibilities.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking about how the depression has affected my ability to function at work and in relationships, including avoiding social situations and missing work, which corresponds directly to the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah... it's definitely affected things. I mean, I haven't had any of those unusual experiences you mentioned, like hearing things or having strange beliefs. It's really just the depression and how heavy everything is. But as far as functioning goes... gosh, it's just been so hard. I try so hard to keep it together, but I've definitely been avoiding social situations. Like, my friends will invite me out for dinner or drinks after work, and I just can't do it. I'll make up excuses, say I'm too tired or I have a headache, because the thought of sitting there and trying to pretend I'm okay, trying to keep up with the conversation and smile when I just feel so incredibly empty and guilty inside... it's just too much. So I just stay home. 

And even at home, things are slipping. I have this townhouse, and I usually take a lot of pride in keeping it nice, but lately, it's just gotten so messy. There are dishes piling up in the sink, laundry sitting in the basket for weeks, and I just look at it and feel even worse about myself, but I can't find the energy to clean it. It's like the mess is just another reminder of how much I'm failing. 

And work... work is where I really feel it. I haven't actually called out or missed days, because I'm so terrified of losing my job, but my performance is definitely suffering. I've been making mistakes, stupid little mistakes that I never used to make. Like, I'll enter the wrong shipping code on an order, or I'll forget to CC a department head on an important update. It got to the point where my supervisor actually pulled me aside and started checking in on me, asking if everything was okay because my error rate was up. That was humiliating. It just reinforced all that guilt I feel. I'm still there, I'm still doing the job, but it takes every ounce of effort I have just to keep up with the basic responsibilities. Everything just feels like it takes ten times more energy than it used to, and I'm just constantly terrified that I'm going to drop a major ball and get fired. It's exhausting.

inference.note: No psychotic or manic features reported, and no suicidal ideation; confirmed marked functional impairment, psychomotor retardation, and insomnia consistent with severe major depressive episode, keeping recurrent MDD and persistent depressive disorder as candidates.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is the patient's first depressive episode or if there were previous, distinct depressive episodes separated by a period of normal mood (to distinguish recurrent MDD from persistent dysthymia)
doctor.question: Before this current two-year period began, had you ever experienced a distinct episode of depression in the past—one that later fully resolved and let you return to feeling like your normal self for a while?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past depressive episodes that occurred before the current two-year period, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not really... I mean, I've been trying to think back to before all this started, and I can't really think of anything like that. Before these last two years, I was actually doing pretty well. I mean, sure, I had normal stress, like anyone else. When I was finishing up my bachelor's degree, there were definitely times I felt completely overwhelmed with finals and trying to figure out what I was going to do with my life. And then starting my job as a business operations specialist... gosh, that was a huge learning curve. I remember my first few months at the company, I was so anxious about making a good impression and learning all the internal systems that I'd stay late almost every single night. 

But even then, even when I was stressed or tired from working long hours, it was never like *this*. It was just normal life stuff, you know? I never had a period where I felt this heavy, awful guilt and sluggishness that just took over my entire life, and then went away. Like, I've never had a time where I sank into a hole like this and then climbed back out and felt totally normal again. It really just feels like... like right around two years ago, this massive, heavy cloud just rolled in, and it's just stayed parked right over my head ever since. 

I really can't point to any time before that where I felt this way and then got better. I was just... normal. I'd go to work, I'd come home, I'd actually enjoy keeping my townhouse tidy, I'd go out with my friends on the weekends without dreading it or making up excuses. I actually had energy. So, no, I haven't had anything like this in the past that just came and went. This is really the first time my life has ever felt this incredibly heavy, and it just... it just hasn't stopped.

inference.note: Patient confirms no prior distinct depressive episodes before this current continuous 2+ year episode, ruling out a recurrent course (F33.1) and making persistent low-grade dysthymia (F34.1) unlikely given the severity of symptoms (psychomotor retardation, significant guilt, sleep disturbance, functional impairment). This presentation is best characterized as a single, severe, chronic major depressive episode without psychotic features (F32.2), though F33.2 remains a differential if the chronicity is later reconceptualized as evolving from subthreshold prior symptoms.

doctor.question: {"intent": "Determine whether the patient has ever had any earlier distinct depressive episode (even a brief, unrecognized one) that fully resolved, to establish whether this is a single lifetime episode or part of a recurrent pattern.", "question": "Thinking back

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past depressive episodes prior to the current 2-year period to determine if this is a recurrent pattern or a single episode. My symptom profile does not contain an item regarding past depressive episodes or recurrence history.

patient.answer:
Thinking back... yeah, I mean, I really have racked my brain about this, probably more than I should. Because you'd think, right? You'd think there would be some warning sign or some earlier time in my life where I felt even a fraction of this, just to kind of prepare me or give me a clue that my brain could do this. But... no. Honestly, no. 

I look back at my teenage years, and I was just a completely standard teenager. I went to dances, I complained about my parents' rules, I worked a part-time job at a little boutique... I never had periods where I couldn't get out of bed or felt this overwhelming, crushing guilt. I was just normal. And then in college... like I was saying before about getting my bachelor's, there was definitely stress. I remember my junior year, I had to take this incredibly intense data analytics seminar, and I was so overwhelmed I literally called my mom hyperventilating, crying my eyes out, saying I was going to fail and drop out and ruin my life. But that lasted, what, maybe a day? I got a good night's sleep, I drank a giant iced coffee the next morning, and I went to the library and just figured it out. It completely resolved. It wasn't depression, it was just... being twenty and stressed about a syllabus. 

And then I went right back to being my normal, hyper-organized self. I was always the friend who planned all our weekend trips, you know? I'd make the detailed itineraries, I'd research the restaurants, I'd book the Airbnbs and figure out the split costs... I had so much energy for all of that. I actually loved doing it. It gave me joy. So there was never a time, not even a brief one, where I just shut down and stopped functioning, or felt this awful, sluggish heaviness, and then magically got better. There was no mini-episode or practice run for this. It's really just this one, long, horrible stretch that started two years ago and never lifted. Before that... I was honestly just fine. I was completely, boringly fine.

inference.note: Patient explicitly denies any prior distinct depressive episode with full remission—this has been one continuous, unremitting episode for over two years. This rules out F33.2 (recurrent depressive disorder), which requires at least two separate episodes. The single, unbroken course with melancholic features (guilt, psychomotor retardation, early morning awakening, anhedonia) supports a single severe depressive episode without psychotic features.
